Girls and women who live in these neighbourhoods rarely come to mind first. A few days after International Women's Day, many people are trying to highlight the work and the realities of women from the neighbourhoods in Montréal and the surrounding area.
Aujourd’hui, certaines d’entre elles par: Today, some of them share their experiences and their views on the women who are forgotten when we talk about women's rights in general, and about the hood in particular.
It's Thursday, the day before March 8. The sun has barely set, and Eya, Amélie, Julie and Adriana join us one after the other for a conversation over dinner. The topic? Girls from the hood. They come from Chomedey, Laval-des-Rapides, Pie-IX and Rivière-des-Prairies respectively, and these four young women are about to discover that they have much more in common than they first thought.
Eya est rappeuse. Vêtue d’un long mantea: Eya is a rapper. Wearing a long black fur coat, she introduces herself: “My artist name is Guessmi – it's also my last name,” she says. Of Tunisian origin, she works in a mostly male industry and understands the reality of girls from the hood better than anyone.
À ses côtés, son amie Amélie l’accompagn: Her friend Amélie is at her side. “I'm 22, I'm from Laval-des-Rapides and I like photography,” she says shyly. A car enthusiast, she works for a car dealership. “When we're on the road together,” the rapper chimes in, “she can name the model, the year, the horsepower and plenty of other details about cars, just by looking at them!”
Les deux amies se sont connues l’été der: The two friends met last summer at an event, and Amélie's love of photography coincided with Eya's desire to produce more visual content for her social media.
Adriana et Julie sont également venues e: Adriana and Julie also came together. At 19, Adriana is an aesthetician specializing in hair removal, and she runs a small marketing agency. Of Haitian and Guatemalan origin, she has lived her whole life in Rivière-des-Prairies. “I did theatre and dance for a very long time,” says the young Montrealer. “But my passion is bubble tea,” she adds with a laugh, half sarcastic, half sincere.
Julie a récemment ouvert PLThé, la bouti: Julie recently opened PLThé, the bubble tea shop where Adriana has just started working. She also owns a beauty and hair salon in Saint-Michel, near where she grew up, and she is the first “Hood Hero” La Converse has profiled. “I'm a Pie-IX girl, I'm an entrepreneur and I'm 30,” she says simply.
Pour la « <em>Hood Hero »</em>, « venir: For the “Hood Hero,” “coming from the hood” is defined by the experience you've had in the neighbourhood. “There are people who live their whole lives in the hood but have never known the realities that the media associate with it,” she begins. Those realities are violence, poverty and crime. “I often hear people say they know people who know people who were victims of violence. Me, I've seen people get shot right in front of me. It affected me directly,” she confides.
Qui dit pluralité des expériences, dit p: Where there are many experiences, there are many opinions. That's the case for these four women, who each see the idea of “success” differently. They explain what success can mean for them as girls from the neighbourhoods.
Lorsqu’on leur demande de nous exposer l: When asked to share their vision of success, Julie doesn't hesitate to speak up. “Success is something very specific to each person. For me, it's how I got to where I am today, when I look at where I come from,” she says proudly. “I'm 30, I'm from another generation,” she says with a laugh. “When I was young, there was a lot of gang activity where I lived. It was very poor. My parents had six jobs between them, and we were even out on the street for a while,” she recalls bitterly.
« Quand tu viens des quartiers, il y a t: “When you come from the neighbourhoods, there's always a label attached to you and to your success. So many times I heard people say I wasn't going to make it because I came from Pie-IX. I understood that, to reach my goals, I had to act and avoid playing the victim,” she says.
Elle explique qu’elle a aussi eu à faire: She explains that she also had to make many sacrifices. “Always working, taking all the money I made to help my parents pay the rent, having several jobs, working seven days a week… it's very hard. I couldn't go out with my friends. While everyone else was chilling, I was working all the time,” she adds firmly.
Malgré tout, Julie est « contente d’avoi: Despite everything, Julie is “glad I did those things.” Today, her success is the sense of accomplishment that colours her days and the pride she inspires in her parents. “Every day, I just want my parents to be proud of me and to be happy,” she finishes, stars in her eyes.
Dans la foulée des propos de Julie, Adri: Following Julie's remarks, Adriana wants to share her own understanding of success. “For other people, I think success is simple: you set a goal, you reach it; that's a success. It can be something tiny in other people's eyes, like brushing your teeth when you were depressed,” she illustrates.
« Personnellement, ma réussite, je l’att: “Personally, I'll have reached success when I've left a legacy for my family. Black women have never had much room in success,” she says. “I want to create my own success and make it so big that my grandchildren won't have to worry about who they are or wonder if they're a problem for society.”
Amélie, presque silencieuse depuis le dé: Amélie, nearly silent until now, shares her vision of success a little later. “For a girl from the hood, I think success is something we've made too big compared to what it can be. Getting out of an unhealthy situation is success. Buying your first car or having your independence is success. It depends on the context,” she says. The Laval resident is alluding to her own story. At 19, she had to leave her family home with almost nothing. “Today, I've managed to get established. I worked hard; I even left school to support myself, but I made it. I have my own place, my independence, my comfort,” she explains. She also says girls “are way too hard on themselves. [We] often see the situation we're living in negatively, and we're less likely to congratulate ourselves and be proud of ourselves and of what we accomplish.”
« Il y a quelques mois, un jeune homme e: “A few months ago, a young man was gunned down right in front of the salon. My employees came to me, panicking at the scene, and me, I acted like nothing was wrong. I told them to keep working, that it was nothing serious!” says Julie.
Elle confie avoir eu besoin de temps pou: She admits it took her time to understand that none of it was normal. “It took me a while. Over the years, I realized that everything I'd lived through when I was younger wasn't the norm,” she confides. “Gunshots were normal to me. But for my employees who come from Longueuil or Laval, it's not normal!”
Cette sinistre introduction pousse les f: This grim opening leads the girls to reflect on the difficulties women in the neighbourhoods face. “It's easier for a guy to talk about his struggles than for a girl. A girl has to deal with more repercussions than a guy,” Eya then says, unfiltered. And all the women present nod in agreement.
Mais où veut-elle en venir ? Elle poursu: But where is she going with this? She keeps going: “I'm talking about my personal experience. In general, even though I've felt it more in my culture as a Maghrebi woman, a woman has to behave, she must never say too much, she has to have a good image,” Eya begins. “I've done some dumb things,” she continues, “but my mother would never accept me going in front of a camera and talking about it. You understand?”
« Je comprends ces femmes qui tendent à: “I understand these women who tend not to put everything out there, the way men would in the hood. It's a vicious cycle, a pattern, and it's very hard to break out of. I also think there's a question of ego, which affects men more than some women,” she adds.
« Penses-tu qu’on excuse plus les conner: “Do you think a guy's screw-ups are excused more?” That's the question put to her right after Eya's last remarks. She answers on the spot: “Of course. A guy with a criminal record is cool, he's a bad boy. A woman with a criminal record has ruined her life. She's tomorrow's mother?” she continues, sarcastic.
Elle est d’ailleurs appuyée dans ses dir: She is backed up by her friend Amélie, sitting right next to her, who wants to point out that the expectations placed on men are very different from those placed on women, especially when it comes to the hardships of life in the neighbourhoods.
« Il y a déjà des attentes bien différen: “There are already very different expectations for men and women in society period. So when you come from a neighbourhood, it's worse,” she begins. “When we think of a girl from the hood who succeeds, we immediately think of an entrepreneur in a super feminine field like aesthetics, but never of a girl in a field like construction or cars,” she compares.
Même si tout parcours a ses hauts et ses: Although every path has its ups and downs, Amélie, who works in the car industry, a very male-dominated one, sees the difference. “We get less applause, we get less encouragement,” she says sadly. “Yet we put in just as much effort to succeed. It's the expectations that are different.”
Lorsqu’on les interroge sur leurs perspe: When asked about their personal prospects in the hood, several hesitate. While Julie has invested in Saint-Michel by opening her salon there, Eya wants to leave the hood. “I've done everything I had to do here,” she says flatly.
Amélie est plus optimiste. Elle insiste: Amélie is more optimistic. She stresses the mutual support among girls of her generation who come from the neighbourhoods, without denying that there are disadvantages to staying in these areas. “The world is small, everybody knows everybody; so it's normal to think you've seen it all and there's nothing left for you,” she says in response to Eya. “But me, in 10 years, I still see myself having a pied-à-terre in Laval-des-Rapides.”
Âgée de 22 ans, elle n’a connu que son q: At 22, she has known only her neighbourhood. “I left my parents' place, but I stayed in the neighbourhood. I'm attached to it, I grew up here, I've spent my whole life here. Even if I hope not to be here 100% of the time,” she says with a laugh, “I'll always want to be able to come back.”
Au début timide, Eya est devenue de plus: Shy at first, Eya grew more and more comfortable over the evening as she kept speaking up. She is also the first to suggest a way forward in response to all the concerns shared by the women around her. “As racialized women, we face difficulties related to being women and being racialized,” she begins by reminding them.
« Il y aura toujours de la misogynie. Il: “There will always be misogyny. We mustn't normalize it, but learn to overcome it,” she says. On the verge of turning 24, the Laval resident acknowledges there's a long road ahead. “I know it sounds extreme, but when you've been through so much, you look at yourself and you can't even bring yourself to ask what needs to be done,” she admits.
Au sujet de ce sentiment d’impuissance,: On this feeling of powerlessness, Julie recalls a friendship that marked her a few years ago. “We were 18. One of my good friends had problems similar to mine related to poverty. She became a dancer to make more money quickly. I told her she shouldn't take that path, but she answered me with something I'll never forget: ‘You're lucky you're good at school, you're lucky you can figure things out and that you're a good salesperson,’” she remembers.
« En fait, on n’a pas toutes les mêmes p: “The truth is, we don't all have the same doors,” Eya realizes right after the entrepreneur's story. Amélie agrees and adds that she has only one wish for the future of girls like her: “I really hope we're going to make it. That we're going to grow personally and as a community.”
